profile.feeling: The question before a verb: what do you…?

collocations.tr: why? (lit. “for what?”) — a word of its own, lesson 10

synonyms.nuance: before nouns and pronouns: مَا هٰذَا؟ مَا اسْمُكَ؟
spoken “what”, after the verb
spoken “what”

etymology.text: From مَا (mā) + ذَا (ḏā).

funFacts: لِمَاذَا, “why”, is literally “for what”.
pitfalls: Use مَاذَا before a verb (مَاذَا تَشْرَبُ؟) but مَا before a noun or pronoun (مَا هٰذَا؟).
subtleties: Formal Arabic also uses مَاذَا before a past verb: مَاذَا فَعَلْتَ؟ (what did you do?).

profile.feeling: Short and frequent — and with many jobs.

synonyms.nuance: the form used before a verb: مَاذَا تَأْكُلُ؟

etymology.text: Cognate with Hebrew מָה (ma) and Ugaritic mh.

funFacts: Hebrew מָה (ma, “what”) is the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: مَا is also the negation “not” (مَا أَكَلْتُ = I didn’t eat) and the relative “what, that which” (أَعْرِفُ مَا تُرِيدُ = I know what you want). Only position and context tell them apart.
subtleties: In the exclamation مَا أَجْمَلَ …! the noun is accusative: مَا أَجْمَلَ الْبَحْرَ!

profile.feeling: Finding your way: places, people, things.

senses.def: where? (also مِنْ أَيْنَ “from where”, إِلَى أَيْنَ “where to”)
how can … compare with …? (أَيْنَ X مِنْ Y — implying there is no comparison)

examples.tr: Where are you from? (to a woman)
How can this even compare with that?

synonyms.nuance: spoken “where”
spoken “where”

etymology.text: From the root ء ي ن (“to come or approach”, “to draw near to a place or time”); related to آن (ʾān, “time, now”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Qurʾān asks: فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ؟ — “So where are you going?” (81:26).
pitfalls: No verb “is” after it: أَيْنَ الْمَحَطَّةُ؟ = where is the station? The noun is nominative.
أَيْنَ always ends in -a; it never takes case endings.
subtleties: أَيْنَمَا + jussive = “wherever”: أَيْنَمَا تَذْهَبْ أَذْهَبْ (wherever you go, I go).

profile.feeling: Asking about people: who?

senses.def: who, the one who; whoever (relative and conditional)

collocations.tr: who is he? / who is she?

phrases.text: مَنْ جَدَّ وَجَدَ، وَمَنْ زَرَعَ حَصَدَ
phrases.tr: whoever strives finds, whoever sows reaps

synonyms.nuance: the spoken “who” of Egypt and the Levant (mīn)
the spoken “who” of Iraq and the Gulf (minū)

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *mann-; cognates include Aramaic מן (man), Geʿez መኑ (männu) and Amharic ማን (man) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Amharic ማን (man), “who”, is the same Semitic word (Wiktionary).
One word for any person: مَنْ does not change for gender or number — مَنْ هُوَ؟ مَنْ هِيَ؟ مَنْ هُمْ؟
pitfalls: Without vowels مَنْ (man, who) and مِنْ (min, from) are both written من — read the context.
مَنْ is for people, مَا / مَاذَا for things: مَنْ هٰذَا؟ (who is this?) but مَا هٰذَا؟ (what is this?).
subtleties: Before al- it takes a helping vowel i: مَنِ الطَّبِيبُ؟ (who is the doctor?).
As a relative or conditional word it means “whoever”: مَنْ جَدَّ وَجَدَ.

profile.feeling: Time and plans: when?

synonyms.nuance: the spoken “when” of Egypt (imta)
the spoken “when” of the Levant (ēmta)

etymology.text: Wiktionary compares مَا (mā, “what?”) and مَنْ (man, “who?”); cognate with Hebrew מָתַי (matai).

funFacts: Hebrew מָתַי (matáy), “when?”, is the same word — one of the easiest bridges between the two languages.
pitfalls: No helper verb and no inversion: مَتَى تَأْكُلُ؟ is literally “when you-eat?”.
Written with ى (alif maqṣūra) but read -ā: matā.
subtleties: With a noun no verb is needed: مَتَى الْعَشَاءُ؟ (When is dinner?) — the noun is nominative.
In formal conditional sentences مَتَى means “whenever”: مَتَى شِئْتَ (whenever you wish).

profile.feeling: Asking after ways and well-being: how?

senses.def: how? (in what way, in what state)

examples.tr: How do you take your coffee?
How do I get to the station?

synonyms.nuance: the spoken “how” of Egypt (izzāy)
pronounced kīf in the Levant and the Maghreb
the spoken “how” of Iraq and the Gulf (šlōn)

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology for the adverb; the noun كَيْف (kayf, “condition, state; mood, pleasure”) is the same word.

funFacts: The noun كَيْف (state, mood, pleasure) went into Turkish as keyif (good mood, pleasure) and from there into Greek as κέφι (kéfi, high spirits).
pitfalls: كَيْفَ asks “how?” — “how many?” is كَمْ and “how much (price)?” is بِكَمْ.
It always ends in -a: kayfa, never with case endings.
subtleties: كَيْفَ + a noun asks after a state: كَيْفَ الْعَمَلُ؟ (How is work?).
كَيْفَمَا = however, in whatever way (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Curiosity and complaint: why?

synonyms.nuance: the short literary form (lima)
the spoken “why” of the Levant and the Gulf (lēš)
the spoken “why” of Egypt (lēh)

etymology.text: From لِـ (li-, “for”) + مَاذَا (māḏā, “what”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Literally “for what?” — built like Greek γιατί (για + τι), Russian почему (по + чему) and Turkish niçin (ne + için).
pitfalls: Written as one word: لِمَاذَا, not *لِ مَاذَا.
The answer starts with لِأَنَّ + a noun or a pronoun ending (لِأَنَّهُ، لِأَنِّي) — that comes in lesson 18.
subtleties: لِمَاذَا لَا …؟ also makes a suggestion: لِمَاذَا لَا نَأْكُلُ هُنَا؟ (Why don’t we eat here?).

profile.feeling: Counting and prices: how many? how much?

senses.def: how many? how much? — followed by a noun in the accusative singular, indefinite (كَمْ أَخًا؟)
how many …! how much …! (exclamation, with مِنْ or a genitive)

examples.tr: How many brothers do you have?
How many books are you buying?

collocations.tr: how old are you? (lit. how much is your age?)

synonyms.nuance: the spoken “how many / how much” of Egypt (kām)
the spoken “how much” of the Levant (qaddēš)

etymology.text: A basic Semitic question word; Wiktionary gives no etymology for it.

funFacts: Hebrew כַּמָּה (kamá), “how many, how much”, is its cousin.
pitfalls: After كَمْ the noun is singular and accusative indefinite: كَمْ أَخًا؟ — not *كَمْ إِخْوَةً؟ (unlike English “how many brothers”).
The price is asked with بِ: بِكَمْ هٰذَا؟ — كَمْ alone asks for a number.
subtleties: Wiktionary: after a preposition (بِكَمْ) the noun may also be genitive — بِكَمْ دِرْهَمٍ؟.
Before al- it takes the helping vowel i: كَمِ السَّاعَةُ؟.

profile.feeling: Choosing among several: which?

senses.def: which? what …? — أَيّ + an indefinite noun in the genitive (أَيُّ كِتَابٍ؟)
any (in questions and negations: أَيُّ شَيْءٍ, anything)

examples.tr: Which house do you live in?

collocations.tr: at any time; at what time

synonyms.nuance: the feminine form, possible before a feminine noun: أَيَّةُ مَدِينَةٍ؟
the spoken “which” of Egypt (anhī)

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔayy- (Wiktionary).

funFacts: أَيّ is the only Arabic question word that declines: أَيُّ, أَيَّ, أَيِّ — it takes the case of its place in the sentence.
pitfalls: The noun after أَيّ is genitive and indefinite: أَيَّ كِتَابٍ, not *أَيَّ الْكِتَابَ.
Its own case depends on its job: subject أَيُّ, object أَيَّ, after a preposition أَيِّ (فِي أَيِّ بَيْتٍ؟).
Not أَيْ (ʾay, “that is, namely”).
subtleties: With a feminine noun both أَيُّ مَدِينَةٍ and أَيَّةُ مَدِينَةٍ are correct; أَيُّ is more common.
With a pronoun ending: أَيُّهُمْ؟ (which of them?), أَيُّهُمَا؟ (which of the two?).

profile.feeling: Who owns it? — whose?

senses.def: whose? (lit. “to whom?”) — لِمَنْ + the thing: لِمَنْ هٰذَا الْكِتَابُ؟

synonyms.nuance: the spoken form in Egypt and the Levant (la-mīn)
Egyptian “whose?” (lit. “belonging to whom?”)

etymology.text: From لِ (li, “for, belonging to”) + مَنْ (man, “who”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: No special word for “whose”: Arabic asks “to whom (is) this book?”, like French à qui est ce livre ? — German wessen and Greek ποιανού are case forms instead.
pitfalls: Answer with لِ + the owner: هٰذَا لِأَبِي (it is my father’s), هٰذَا لِي (it is mine) — لِي, never *لِأَنَا.
subtleties: Also correct: كِتَابُ مَنْ هٰذَا؟ (whose book is this?), with مَنْ as the second word of a construct.
Before al- it takes the helping vowel i: لِمَنِ الْكِتَابُ؟.

profile.feeling: Trust and respect — a career many families dream of for their children.

examples.tr: My sister is a doctor at the hospital.
I’m ill — I need a doctor.
The doctor is at the practice today.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word and form of address (duktūr / doktōr): يَا دُكْتُورُ
literally “wise man”; the old word for a doctor, still heard in the Levant and Egypt

etymology.text: From the root ط ب ب (ṭ b b, “medicine”: طِبّ), on the pattern faʿīl; Wiktionary gives no older etymology.

funFacts: طِبّ (ṭibb, medicine) is the same root: Turkish tıp (medicine) and tabip (physician) come from it.
pitfalls: The plural is broken and a diptote: أَطِبَّاءُ (no tanwīn), not *طَبِيبُونَ; women doctors are طَبِيبَات.
subtleties: In speech a doctor is addressed as دُكْتُور / دُكْتُورَة; طَبِيب is the word for the profession.
Wiktionary also lists the rarer plural أَطِبَّة.

profile.feeling: Care and patience at the bedside.

examples.tr: The nurse is helping the doctor.
My brother works as a nurse in the hospital.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: مُمَرِّض / مُمَرِّضَة is the standard word everywhere; nursing is التَّمْرِيض.

etymology.text: Active participle of the form II verb مَرَّضَ (marraḍa, “to nurse, to tend the sick”), from the root م ر ض (m r ḍ, “illness”) (Wiktionary root).

funFacts: The same root gives مَرِيض (ill; a patient) and مَرَض (illness): the nurse is “the one who tends the ill”.
pitfalls: Most nurses in the Arab world are women, so you will hear مُمَرِّضَة far more often — a male nurse is مُمَرِّض.
Do not confuse it with مَرِيض (marīḍ, ill, a patient): same root, the other side of the bed.
subtleties: The pattern mufaʿʿil (مُمَرِّض, مُعَلِّم) names someone who does something for others.

profile.feeling: Bridges, buildings and machines — a prestigious profession.

examples.tr: She is an engineer at a big company.
The engineers are building a new bridge.

synonyms.nuance: Egyptian honorific address to an engineer (from Turkish baş, “chief”)

etymology.text: From the root ه ن د س (h n d s), from هَنْدَسَة (handasa, “geometry, architecture, engineering”), from earlier هَنْدَزَة, from هَنْدَاز, borrowed from Middle Persian handāz- (“to plan, reckon”) or handāzag (“measure”) (> Persian andâze) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Turkish mühendis (engineer) is this Arabic word; its Persian source survives in Persian andâze, “measure”.
pitfalls: Four root letters (ه ن د س): the plural is sound, مُهَنْدِسُونَ — no broken plural.
subtleties: هَنْدَسَة is both “engineering” and “geometry”; Wiktionary also lists the older senses “geometer, architect, surveyor”.

profile.feeling: Taxis, buses and long roads.

examples.tr: The driver is waiting in front of the house.
My brother is a bus driver.

synonyms.nuance: the spoken word (sawwāq), above all in Egypt

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of سَاقَ (sāqa, “to drive”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: سَاقَ first meant driving animals before you; the verbal noun سَوْق is now also “driving (a car)” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The hamza sits on a yāʾ seat: سَائِق (sāʾiq); spoken Arabic often says sāyiq.
Wiktionary lists the plurals سَائِقُونَ, سَاقَة and سُوَّاق; the sound سَائِقُونَ is the safe one.
subtleties: The fāʿil pattern makes “the one who does”: سَائِق (driver), طَالِب (student), بَائِع (seller).

profile.feeling: Pots, spices and a busy kitchen.

examples.tr: My grandfather was a cook in a restaurant.
The cook is cooking the fish.
My mother is a skilled cook.

synonyms.nuance: cook, chef — the formal written word
chef (from French), in restaurants and on television

etymology.text: From the root ط ب خ (ṭ b ḫ); cognate with Hebrew טַבָּח (tabbaḥ, “butcher, cook”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: faʿʿāl is the pattern of trades: طَبَّاخ (cook), خَبَّاز (baker), نَجَّار (carpenter), فَنَّان (artist).
Hebrew טַבָּח (tabach, cook) has the same root and the same pattern.
pitfalls: The bāʾ is doubled (šadda): ṭabbāḫ; خ is the ch of German Bach.
subtleties: At home one says أُمِّي تَطْبُخُ (my mother cooks); طَبَّاخ is the profession — or someone known as a good cook.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses بَائِع as “seller”; the concept’s shop assistant / salesperson is the seller in a shop, and Wiktionary has no separate sense for it.

profile.feeling: Shops and market stalls: the person behind the counter.

examples.tr: The shop assistant in this shop is nice.
He sells vegetables at the market.
My sister is a shop assistant in a clothes shop.

synonyms.nuance: sales employee — in companies and job adverts
merchant, trader — the owner of the business rather than the assistant

etymology.text: Active participle of بَاعَ (bāʕa, “to sell”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The market pair: بَائِع (seller, from بَاعَ) and مُشْتَرٍ (buyer, from اِشْتَرَى — the verb of lesson 7).
pitfalls: Two masculine plurals: بَاعَة (common for vendors: الْبَاعَةُ) and the sound بَائِعُونَ; women: بَائِعَات.
The hamza sits on a yāʾ seat: بَائِع (bāʾiʿ).
subtleties: The shop owner is صَاحِبُ الْمَحَلِّ, the merchant تَاجِر; بَائِع is whoever sells to you.

profile.feeling: Factories, building sites and the 1st of May.

examples.tr: My father is a worker in a factory.
The workers are building a new house.

examples.text: عِيدُ الْعُمَّالِ فِي الْأَوَّلِ مِنْ مَايُو.
examples.tr: Labour Day is on the first of May.

synonyms.nuance: employee, office worker (white-collar)
hired hand, day labourer

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of عَمِلَ (ʕamila, “to do, to act, to work”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same root gives عَمَل (work) — a place word of the next lesson; Turkish amele (labourer) comes from the Arabic plural عَمَلَة.
pitfalls: “Workers” is usually the broken plural عُمَّال; عَوَامِل is the plural of the other عَامِل, “factor”.
subtleties: عَامِل is manual or factory work; an office employee is مُوَظَّف.

profile.feeling: Fields, harvests and early mornings — the neutral, modern word.

examples.tr: My grandfather is a farmer in a small village.
The farmer sells vegetables at the market.

synonyms.nuance: farmer, peasant who works the land himself — traditional and rural (above all in Egypt)

etymology.text: Occupational noun from the root ز ر ع (z r ʕ, “sowing”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The root ز ر ع gives زَرَعَ (to sow, to plant), زِرَاعَة (agriculture) and مَزْرَعَة (farm); Hebrew זֶרַע (zera, seed) is a cognate.
pitfalls: مُزَارِع (muzāriʿ, a farmer) vs مَزَارِع (mazāriʿ, farms — plural of مَزْرَعَة): one vowel makes the difference.
subtleties: مُزَارِع is the neutral modern word (farm owner, agricultural worker); فَلَّاح evokes the traditional peasant.
Wiktionary gives no feminine; مُزَارِعَة (plural مُزَارِعَات) is the regular feminine used for women farmers.

profile.feeling: The peasant of the Nile valley and the village fields.

examples.text: الْفَلَّاحُ يَعْمَلُ فِي الْحَقْلِ مِنَ الصَّبَاحِ.
examples.tr: The farmer has been working in the field since the morning.

examples.text: جَدِّي فَلَّاحٌ مِنْ قَرْيَةٍ فِي مِصْرَ.
examples.tr: My grandfather is a farmer from a village in Egypt.
The farmers sell vegetables at the market.

synonyms.nuance: farmer — the modern, neutral word

etymology.text: From the root ف ل ح (f l ḥ). The sense “farmer” is assumed to be borrowed from Aramaic pallāḥā (“worker; peasant”), since Aramaic speakers farmed while most Arabic speakers were nomads; فَلَحَ (“to plough”) would then come from the noun (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The call to prayer says حَيَّ عَلَى الْفَلَاحِ, “come to success”: فَلَاح (success) has the same letters, with a single l.
pitfalls: فَلَّاح (fallāḥ, doubled l) = farmer; فَلَاح (falāḥ) = success, salvation.
In some contexts فَلَّاح can sound condescending (“peasant, yokel”); مُزَارِع is the safe neutral word.
subtleties: Two words, one concept: مُزَارِع for farming as a profession, فَلَّاح for the traditional peasant — the profile of each says which.

profile.feeling: Uniforms, traffic and order in the streets.

examples.tr: The police officer is in the street.
My brother is a police officer in the city.

synonyms.nuance: policeman (lit. “man of the police”) — very common, plural رِجَالُ الشُّرْطَةِ
police, policeman (from French police), in Egypt and elsewhere

etymology.text: From شُرْطَة (šurṭa, “police”) + the nisba suffix ـِيّ (-iyy) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The nisba ending -iyy makes “one belonging to”: شُرْطَة → شُرْطِيّ (policeman), like مِصْر → مِصْرِيّ (Egyptian).
pitfalls: The final yāʾ is doubled: شُرْطِيٌّ (šurṭiyyun), accusative شُرْطِيًّا.
Wiktionary gives two vowelings: šurṭiyy (شُرْطِيّ) and šuraṭiyy (شُرَطِيّ).
subtleties: The plural شُرْطِيُّونَ is correct, but people more often say رِجَالُ الشُّرْطَةِ (“men of the police”).

profile.feeling: Courtrooms and contracts: the one who defends you.

examples.tr: The lawyer is in court today.

synonyms.nuance: legal adviser
attorney, legal representative; also an agent in general

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of حَامَى (ḥāmā, “to defend”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Literally “the defender”: the same root ح م ي gives حِمَايَة (protection).
pitfalls: A defective noun: مُحَامٍ (muḥāmin) without the article, الْمُحَامِي (al-muḥāmī) with it, accusative مُحَامِيًا — the ī appears only when something follows it.
Spoken Arabic says muḥāmi everywhere, and you will often see the spelling مُحَامِي even without the article.
subtleties: The feminine is regular: مُحَامِيَة, مُحَامِيَات; the masculine plural is sound: مُحَامُونَ / مُحَامِينَ.

profile.feeling: Painters, singers and actors — the world of فَنّ, art.

examples.tr: My brother is an artist; he paints every day.

synonyms.nuance: painter, illustrator
singer — though singers are very often called فَنَّان

etymology.text: Occupational noun from فَنّ (fann, “art”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: In the Arab world الْفَنَّانُ … very often introduces a singer or an actor; Turkish fen (science, technique) is the same word فَنّ.
pitfalls: The n is doubled: فَنَّان (fannān) — the faʿʿāl pattern of professions.
subtleties: فَنّ (art) has the plural فُنُون: كُلِّيَّةُ الْفُنُونِ الْجَمِيلَةِ (faculty of fine arts).
